lessons.title: if, else and comparisons
lessons.summary: Making a program choose between two paths.
lessons.notes:
**Selection** means the program picks which lines to run.

```python
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")
else:
    print("Child")
```

Comparison operators: `==` equal to, `!=` not equal to, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.

Two classic mistakes:
- using `=` (assignment) when you mean `==` (comparison)
- forgetting the colon or the indentation under the `if`
lessons.worked_example_note: Only one of the two `print` lines can ever run. The indented block belongs to the branch above it.

lessons.title: elif chains and logical operators
lessons.summary: More than two options, and conditions joined with and/or/not.
lessons.notes:
Use `elif` for a chain of options. Python checks them in order and stops at the first one that is true, so **order matters** — put the strictest boundary first.

```python
if mark >= 80:
    grade = "9"
elif mark >= 60:
    grade = "7"
else:
    grade = "4"
```

Join conditions with `and` (both must be true), `or` (at least one), `not` (reverses it).

OCR wording tip: *"between 10 and 20 inclusive"* becomes `if 10 <= n <= 20:` or `if n >= 10 and n <= 20:`.
lessons.worked_example_note: `and` needs both sides to be true. Compare strings with `==` and remember they are case sensitive.

lessons.title: Exam-style selection problems
lessons.summary: Working out the boundaries from a written scenario.
lessons.notes:
Exam scenarios hide the conditions inside sentences. Build a small table before you code:

```text
Condition          Output
90 or more         Gold
70 to 89           Silver
less than 70       Bronze
```

Then write one branch per row, strictest first. Check the **boundary values** (exactly 90, exactly 70) — that is where marks are usually lost.
lessons.worked_example:
# Discount: 10% off orders of 50 or more, 5% off orders of 20 or more
total = float(input())
if total >= 50:
    total = total * 0.9
elif total >= 20:
    total = total * 0.95
print(round(total, 2))
lessons.worked_example_note: There is no `else` here because orders under £20 need no change at all.

tasks.title: Positive or negative
tasks.brief: Read a whole number. Print `Positive` if it is greater than 0, otherwise print `Not positive`.
hints: Use `if n > 0:` and `else:`

tasks.title: Old enough to vote
tasks.brief: Read an age. Print `Can vote` if the age is 18 or more, otherwise print `Too young`.
hints: 18 or more means `>= 18`

tasks.title: Bigger of two
tasks.brief: Read two whole numbers on separate lines. Print the larger one. If they are equal, print `Equal`.
hints: Check the equal case with `elif a == b:`

tasks.title: Traffic light
tasks.brief: A program reads the colour of a traffic light. Print `Stop` for `red`, `Get ready` for `amber` and `Go` for `green`. For anything else print `Broken`.
hints: An if / elif / elif / else chain
Compare the string exactly

tasks.title: In range
tasks.brief: Read a whole number. Print `In range` if it is between 10 and 20 inclusive, otherwise print `Out of range`.
hints: Inclusive means 10 and 20 both count
`10 <= n <= 20` works in Python

tasks.title: Login with two checks
tasks.brief: Read a username then a password. Print `Welcome` only if the username is `admin` and the password is `hcode`. Otherwise print `Rejected`.
hints: Join the two conditions with `and`

tasks.title: Swimming pool entry
tasks.brief: A swimming pool charges different prices by age. Children under 5 swim free, anyone under 16 pays £2, adults pay £4 and anyone aged 65 or over pays £2. The program should accept a person's age and display the price they pay as a whole number of pounds, for example `2`.
hints: Deal with the youngest ages first
Remember the over-65 case comes before the adult case, or check it separately

tasks.title: Parcel size checker
tasks.brief: A courier classifies parcels by weight in kilograms. Parcels up to and including 2 kg are `Small`, over 2 kg and up to 10 kg are `Medium`, and anything heavier is `Large`. Parcels weighing more than 30 kg are refused and should display `Refused` instead. Read the weight as a decimal and display the classification.
hints: Check the refusal case before the Large case
Watch the boundaries: exactly 2 and exactly 10

tasks.title: Quiz feedback
tasks.brief: A quiz is marked out of 20. The program should take the mark scored and report a comment: `Excellent` for 18 or more, `Good` for 14 to 17, `Pass` for 10 to 13 and `Revise this topic` for anything lower. Marks outside the range 0 to 20 should display `Invalid mark`.
hints: Validate the mark first, before grading it
Order the grade boundaries from highest down

tasks.title: Theme park ride restrictions
tasks.brief:
A theme park needs software to check whether a visitor may ride a rollercoaster.

A visitor may ride if they are at least 140 cm tall **and** aged 12 or over. Visitors who are tall enough but too young may ride if they are accompanied by an adult.

The program accepts three lines of input: the height in centimetres (whole number), the age (whole number), and then `yes` or `no` to say whether an adult is with them.

It must output one of:
- `Ride allowed`
- `Ride allowed with adult`
- `Ride refused`
hints: Deal with the height rule first — too short is always refused
Then split on age, then on the adult answer

tasks.title: Broadband billing
tasks.brief:
An internet provider bills customers monthly.

The standard package costs £25 per month and includes 100 GB of data. Any data used above the 100 GB allowance is charged at £1.50 per whole gigabyte over the limit.

Customers who have been with the provider for 24 months or more receive a 10% discount on the **whole** bill.

Write a program that accepts the gigabytes used (a whole number) followed by the number of months the customer has been with the provider, then outputs the final bill rounded to 2 decimal places, for example `Bill: £32.50`.
hints: Excess data is only charged when usage is above 100
Apply the loyalty discount after adding the excess charge

tasks.title: Library fine system
tasks.brief:
A school library charges fines for late books.

Books returned up to 3 days late are not fined. From day 4 onwards the fine is 20p per day late, counting **all** the days late, not just those after day 3. The fine is capped at £5.00 no matter how late the book is.

Students in Year 7 are never fined.

The program accepts the number of days late (a whole number) then the student's year group (a whole number), and outputs the fine in pounds to 2 decimal places, for example `Fine: £1.0`.
hints: Check the Year 7 rule first — it overrides everything
Cap with something like `if fine > 5: fine = 5`
